task: Nothing is selected; the user takes the one action the empty panel offers.
finding: With nothing selected the panel shows one sentence and one action, '✦ Ask AI ›'. That action does not open a side panel — it REPLACES the inspector with the AI tab, and nothing brings the inspector back except the AI tab's own '‹ Back'. Selecting an element on the canvas afterwards does not restore it: the right column stays on AI while the canvas shows a selected element with a selection box, and every style control for that element is unreachable until the user notices the small Back control. The same trap is one click away from a populated inspector too (the '✦ AI' chip in the element header).
evidence: InspectorEmptyState.tsx:90 emits ui:switch-tab {tab:'ai'}; ProInspector.tsx:378 the header chip emits the same; StudioPanels.tsx:291-302 the handler routes tab==='ai' to setAiInInspector(true); StudioPanels.tsx:495-501 shows AITab in the inspector slot and clears the flag ONLY from onClose/onBack. Searched: 'aiInInspector', 'setAiInInspector', 'ui:switch-tab', EVENTS.UI_SWITCH_TAB, 'ELEMENT_SELECTED' (no listener resets it).
fix: Selecting an element must return the right column to the inspector (or the AI panel must dock beside the inspector, not over it). At minimum the AI takeover needs a persistent 'Back to properties' header, not a chevron.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: A user selects a locked element from the Layers tree and tries to edit it.
finding: The canvas refuses to select a locked element and toasts 'This element is locked. Unlock it in the Layers panel.' The Layers tree has no such check — clicking a locked layer selects it — and the inspector then renders EVERY control fully enabled, with no lock badge in the header, no banner, and no Unlock action. The header's crosshair 'Pick element on canvas' is a second back door: pick mode calls selection.select() directly with no lock check. So the product tells the user an element cannot be edited and then gives them two ways to edit it.
evidence: useSelectionBehavior.ts:88,106,134 block the locked element with a toast; useLayerSelection.ts:67-72 selectSingle and :76+ selectLayer call composer.selection.select/toggle with no isLocked() test; Canvas.tsx:608-617 pick mode selects with no isLocked() test; Element.ts:394 / ElementSerialization.ts:140 isLocked(). Searched inside packages/editor/src/editor/inspector for 'locked', 'isLocked', 'lock' — the only hits are the word 'block' inside CSS display values and one comment in InspectorTabContent.tsx:229.
fix: Either the Layers tree refuses selection the way the canvas does, or the inspector shows a locked state: a header lock badge, controls disabled, and one 'Unlock' button that clears data.locked in place.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user shift-selects several elements and tries to work on them together.
finding: Two or more selected replaces the whole inspector with a toolbar: a '3 selected' count, 6 align buttons, 2 distribute buttons and 5 batch fields (background, text colour, radius, padding, font size). There is no list of WHAT is selected — no names, no types, no way to drop one item out of the selection from here; no delete; no group/wrap; and no scope / breakpoint / state pill row, so the user cannot see which layer the batch write lands on. It lands on the canvas's current device: with the canvas on Tablet, every batch edit writes a tablet-only override and the panel says nothing.
evidence: ProInspector.tsx:298-310 short-circuits to MultiSelectToolbar BEFORE the bdi-bpr pill row at :420-444; MultiSelectToolbar.tsx:213-336 is the whole panel; BatchStylePanel.tsx:97-123 is the five fields, :70-71 defaults currentBreakpoint/currentPseudoState from props; useBatchStyleHandler is passed the live breakpoint at MultiSelectToolbar.tsx:333-335. Searched: 'MultiSelectToolbar', 'isMultiSelect', 'selectedIds.length > 1', 'BatchStylePanel'.
fix: Multi-select needs the same context header the single selection has (breakpoint + state pill at minimum), a list of the selected items with per-row remove, and the destructive/structural actions (delete, group) the single-selection ⋯ menu already has.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user picks 'All like this' to restyle every button at once.
finding: The scope dropdown's own copy scopes the fan-out to the current page — 'no other buttons on this page', 'no other buttons here' — but the peer set comes from the element registry, which the engine documents as accumulating EVERY loaded page and never clearing except on a full project reset. So 'All like this' can silently repaint buttons on About and Contact while the user is looking at Home, and the banner only ever says a number ('Editing all 12 buttons'), never which pages they are on.
evidence: ScopeDropdown.tsx:58-67 peers = composer.elements.getAllElements().filter(same type); :153 title 'No other ${typeLabel}s on this page'; :159 'no other ${typeLabel}s here'. ElementManager.ts:151-163 getAllElements: 'Get every registered element, across all loaded pages' and :530-533 'setActivePage… never clears or repopulates this registry — the only clear() is a full project reset'. Same filter reused for the writes at ProInspector.tsx:119-131 → useStyleHandlers.ts:262 writeOne(peerId). Searched: 'getAllElements', 'getActivePage', 'reachPeerIds', 'reachAll'.
fix: Either scope the peer set to the active page (and say so), or keep it project-wide and say THAT — 'also changes 9 buttons on 3 other pages', with a way to see them before committing.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user turns on 'All like this', edits one button, then clicks the next button to keep going.
finding: 'All like this' is a mode with a banner that is supposed to stay up while you work, but it is reset by any change of selection. Clicking the next button of the same type — the most likely next action inside this mode — silently drops back to 'This item': banner gone, pill back to 'This', and the next edit lands on one element only. Nothing tells the user the mode ended.
evidence: ProInspector.tsx:110-114 useEffect([selectedElement?.id]) calls setReachAll(false) (and setWholeSite(false)); the banner at :462-474 and the peer set at :119-131 both key off reachAll. Searched: 'reachAll', 'onReachAllChange', 'setReachAll'.
fix: Keep the reach mode across selection changes of the same element type (it is a working mode, not a property of one element), and end it explicitly — or, if it must reset, say so in the banner as it goes.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user picks 'Whole site' from the scope dropdown.
finding: The body is replaced by a card reading 'Editing the whole site — every page' while the pill directly above it still reads 'This'. The panel's own code comments call exactly this contradiction unacceptable for the reach mode, then leave it standing for the site mode. The state is also lost on any selection change, and the card is not really an editing mode at all — it is a signpost to the Brand panel, so the scope dropdown offers a third 'reach' that has no controls behind it.
evidence: ScopeDropdown.tsx:113 label is `reachAll ? 'All like this' : 'This'` — wholeSite is never passed in; ProInspector.tsx:99 owns wholeSite, :518-537 renders the takeover card, :112 resets it on selection change; the comment at ScopeDropdown.tsx:109-112 states 'a control that misreports its own state is the worse half to keep'. task: Anyone looking for the controls the product's own config says exist.
finding: VERIFIED, and larger than the prior finding said. 'data.repeaterEnabled' is registered with no renderer — but so is the entire registry: PROPERTIES holds 185 property definitions across 31 families and NOTHING imports it. It is re-exported from config/index.ts and read by no section, no renderer and no hook. Whole families describe product surfaces that appear in no panel: slider.* (8: slides, autoplay, navUI, loop, drag, pauseOnHover…), modal.* (8), navbar.* (7: menuItems, logo, sticky, mobileCollapse…), tabs.* (6), accordion.* (6), data.* (8: collection, bindField, repeaterEnabled, mapping, filters, sort, limit, emptyState), a11y.* (5), visibilityRules.* (4), form.* (4).
evidence: propertiesRegistry.ts:877 '"data.repeaterEnabled": { uiOnly: true, type: "toggle" … }'; the map runs propertiesRegistry.ts:100-1093 (185 keys counted by parsing the export); config/index.ts:19-22 re-exports PROPERTIES; grep for 'PROPERTIES' across packages/editor/src/editor/inspector returns only that re-export and the unrelated ELEMENT_PROPERTIES in sections/elementProperties/config.ts. Searched: 'PROPERTIES', 'propertiesRegistry', 'getPropertyDefinition', 'isAdvancedProperty', 'from "../config"'. Note registry/index.tsx:120-131 deliberately stopped asking this registry for advanced props ('Sections declare what they draw').
fix: Delete the registry, or make it the source the sections render from. Leaving it as the only written description of the intended inspector guarantees every future audit re-discovers features that do not exist.

screen: Inspector · slider / tabs / accordion / navbar element
task: The user inserts a Slider (or Tabs, Accordion, Navbar) from Insert and selects it to configure it.
finding: These composite elements have no component-level editor. Every one of them falls through to the generic container profile, and the only non-style section they get is 'Element properties', which for them contains three raw HTML attributes: ID, Title, Tab Index. There is no way to add or remove a slide, set autoplay, choose arrows vs dots, add an accordion item, set single-vs-multiple open, or edit navbar menu items — the user has to select the generated child elements one at a time in Layers and hand-build the structure.
evidence: elementProfiles.ts:231-241 slider/accordion/navbar/table/list all map to CONTAINER_PROFILE; 'tabs' is not a key at all so getProfileFor falls back (elementProfiles.ts:283-297); sections/elementProperties/config.ts:24-330 has no slider/tabs/accordion/navbar entry, so getPropertiesForType (:331-334) returns only ELEMENT_PROPERTIES.default = id / title / tabindex (:316-320). The Insert catalog does offer the block: catalog.ts:476-478 blockId 'slider'. Searched: 'slidesEditor', 'itemsEditor', 'menuEditor', 'Add slide', 'Add tab', 'accordion item', "'slider'" across packages/editor/src.
fix: Give composite elements a first section that edits the component, not its CSS: an item list with add/remove/reorder plus the two or three behaviour switches. This is the one place a builder differs from a CSS panel.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user drops a contact form on the page and tries to say where submissions go.
finding: Selecting a form gives Action URL, Method, Encoding, Disable Validation and Autocomplete — five raw HTML attributes. There is no field for an email address, a webhook, a success message or a redirect, so a non-technical user has no way to make the form actually deliver anything. The section that WOULD do this exists and is finished: FormSettingsSection, whose own header says 'Inspector section for form element configuration', wires to the engine's FormHandler, and is exported from the shared/forms barrel — and it is mounted nowhere.

Searched: 'FormSettingsSection', '<FormSettingsSection', 'submitAction', 'formConfig', 'useFormHandler'.
fix: Mount FormSettingsSection in the form element's profile (or fold its fields into Element properties). Whatever the fix, the form's destination must be editable without knowing what an 'action URL' is.

task: The user knows the property they want ('z-index', 'letter spacing', 'object fit') and tries to find it.
finding: There is no search field anywhere in the inspector. A container's profile lists 16 sections, most of them collapsed, several with a further 'More settings' disclosure inside them — so finding one property means opening sections one at a time and guessing which family owns it. The plumbing for search exists and is inert: useAdvancedSettings takes a searchQuery and auto-expands the advanced group that matches, and ProInspector passes the empty string, permanently.

task: The user wants to see everything set on this element, or to shut the panel back down.
finding: There is no expand-all or collapse-all in the inspector. On first sight the panel opens only the sections that carry a value, which is a good default, but the remaining 10-13 sections can only be opened one click at a time and there is no way to sweep them shut again. Both functions are implemented, scoped correctly to the selected element's profile, persisted to localStorage — and called by nothing.

The only expandAll/collapseAll wired to a control in the app is the Layers panel's (panels/layers/index.tsx:48-59). Searched: 'expandAll', 'collapseAll', 'Expand all', 'Collapse all' across packages/editor/src.

task: The user sees a greyed-out field and wants to know why.
finding: The panel computes a plain-English reason for every disabled property ('Inline elements ignore vertical spacing', 'Set position to relative/absolute/fixed to edit offsets') and then mostly throws it away. Spacing passes only a boolean down, so on an inline element four margin/padding boxes go grey with no explanation at all. Where the reason IS passed it is a native title= on a DISABLED input, and browsers suppress pointer events on disabled form controls, so the tooltip does not open. The net effect for the user is dead controls with no cause and no route to fixing the cause.
evidence: cssContext.ts:150-197 getPropertyStates builds { disabled, reason }; SpacingSection.tsx:97-98 and :248-259 forward only `?.disabled` — SpacingControls.tsx:121-148 has no reason prop and AxisInput (:50-87) sets only `disabled`; PositionControls.tsx:150,162,172,184 put reason() in title= on a disabled TextInput; FlexItemControls.tsx:61,75,89 do the same; SizeSection.tsx:188,221,252,268,289,305 pass disabledReason. Searched: 'propertyStates', 'reason', 'disabledReason', 'title={reason'.
fix: Show the reason as visible helper text under the disabled row, and make it actionable where possible ('Set position to relative' as a one-click button, the way Flexbox's EnableFlexPrompt already does for display:flex).
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: A user wants gap, or wants to control how one child stretches inside its flex parent.
finding: Two of the four disabled reasons can never be seen, because the controls they explain are not rendered at all. Gap lives inside the `isFlexContainer &&` branch and the flex-item block inside `isFlexItem &&`, so on a plain div the user sees no gap row and no grow/shrink/basis/align-self row — not a disabled one with 'Enable flex/grid to use gaps' or 'Applies only to flex items'. The controls simply are not there, so the user has no way to learn that they exist or what unlocks them. (The one good counter-example is in the same file: EnableFlexPrompt, which appears when the container is not flex.)
evidence: cssContext.ts:173-186 writes reasons for gap/row-gap/column-gap and flex-grow/shrink/basis/align-self/order; flexbox/index.tsx:100-166 wraps GapControls in `{isFlexContainer && …}` and :169-176 wraps FlexItemControls in `{isFlexItem && …}`; the disabled/reason helpers at :63-64 are therefore only reachable for rows that are already visible. Searched: 'isFlexItem', 'isFlexContainer', 'GapControls', 'FlexItemControls', 'Enable flex'.
fix: Render the row disabled with its reason instead of hiding it, exactly as the Position offsets do — a control the user can see and cannot use teaches; a missing control does not.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user wants the element to fade in.
finding: The panel has TWO animation systems, adjacent in every element profile, that do not acknowledge each other. 'Interactions' adds a trigger (14 of them) plus one of 39 presets and runs on the GSAP runtime. 'Animation' has no trigger at all, offers 25 presets in three tabs (Entrance / Attention / Exit), allows exactly one per element, and writes the CSS animation property. Sixteen presets appear in both lists with the same label (Fade In, Zoom In, Pulse, Bounce, Shake, Swing, Wobble, Flash, Heartbeat, Rubber Band, Rotate In, Slide In Up/Down, Fade Out, Zoom Out), and each list has presets the other lacks. Nothing in either section says when to use which, whether they conflict on one element, or which one runs on the published page.
evidence: elementProfiles.ts (every profile) orders … effects, interactions, animation, visibility …; sections/interactions/types.ts:95-147 ANIMATION_PRESET_GROUPS = 6 groups / 39 presets (fade 6, slide 6, scale 6, rotate 6, attention 8, special 7) and :69-92 TRIGGER_GROUPS = 4 groups / 14 triggers — both counts verified; editor/animation/AnimationEditor.tsx:21-53 animations = entrance 12 / attention 8 / exit 5 = 25; AnimationSection.tsx:61-69 one config per element, no trigger; registry/effects.tsx:22-126 registers both. Searched: 'ANIMATION_PRESET_GROUPS', 'ANIMATION_PRESETS', 'AnimationEditor', 'InteractionsSection'.
fix: One motion section. A trigger of 'On page load' is what 'Animation' actually is; fold it in as a trigger and keep one preset catalogue.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user has added a trigger and now picks what should happen.
finding: The 39 presets are grouped into six named families in the constants — and the only thing that renders them is a single flat <select> built from the flattened list, so the grouping is thrown away at the point of use. The user scrolls one 39-item dropdown of bare names (Jello, Tada, Hinge, Roll In, Rubber Band) with no preview of any kind; the only way to see what a preset does is to choose it, close the dropdown, and press Preview. Choosing between 'Slide Up' and 'Fade In Up' and 'Slide In Up' by name is guesswork.

Repo grep for ANIMATION_PRESET_GROUPS outside types.ts returns only the coverage test (__tests__/presetCoverage.test.ts:17). task: The user clicks '+ Add Interaction' and picks when the animation should fire.
finding: Fourteen triggers appear at once in a 2-column grid under four headings, each a bare label with an emoji and no description, and several of them are indistinguishable to a user: 'On Hover' vs 'Mouse Over', 'Mouse Out' vs 'On Blur', and three separate scroll answers ('Page Scroll', 'Scroll Into View', 'While Scrolling', plus 'Scroll Out'). Nothing is filtered by element type, so a plain container is offered 'On Focus' and 'On Blur', and every element on the page is offered its own 'Page Load' and 'Page Leave'. There is also no duplicate guard — adding 'On Hover' twice is allowed and produces two rows with the same title.
evidence: types.ts:69-92 the 14 triggers in 4 groups; AddInteractionPanel.tsx:98-133 renders every group as a 2-col grid of label+icon buttons, no descriptions, no filtering, no search; interactions/index.tsx:57-68 addInteraction appends unconditionally; InteractionItem.tsx:82-84 shows icon + trigger label + preset only. Searched: 'TRIGGER_GROUPS', 'GROUP_LABELS', 'AddInteractionPanel', 'getTriggerInfo'.
fix: Cut the list to what applies to this element type, describe each trigger in a line, and collapse the near-synonyms (one 'When it scrolls into view' rather than three scroll triggers a user must A/B).

screen: Inspector · footer 'N of M sections apply'
task: The user reads the line that explains why most of the panel is shut.
finding: The footer counts a section as 'applying' only if the element carries a value for one of the CSS keys the section declares — but six of the sections in a text element's profile declare no CSS keys at all (link, interactions, animation, element-properties, css-classes, all-css), so they are structurally incapable of ever counting, no matter how much the user has configured in them. An element with three interactions and four classes still reads '2 of 13 sections apply'. The denominator also includes sections that are always empty-ish: 'Element properties' on a container is three raw HTML attributes and never returns nothing, so it is always in M and never in N.
evidence: registry/index.tsx:102-111 sectionApplies() reads entry.styleKeys; registry/element.tsx:16,34,52,64 all set styleKeys: []; registry/effects.tsx:23,81 animation and interactions likewise; InspectorTabContent.tsx:220-225 renders the count over renderIds; elementProperties/config.ts:316-320 the always-present default trio. Searched: 'sectionApplies', 'styleKeys', 'sections apply'.
fix: Either let a section report its own 'has content' (an interactions count, a class count) or stop counting sections that own no CSS in the denominator. As written the line understates the element every time.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user hides an element on mobile.
finding: The Visibility section writes a custom property (--hide-mobile) that neither of the CSS keys its registry entry declares has anything to do with. Two consequences the user feels: the section auto-opens and is counted as 'applying' whenever the element merely has a display or opacity value, i.e. almost always; and an element whose ONLY setting is 'hidden on mobile' does not count as applying and does not auto-open, so the one thing configured about it is the one thing that stays shut. The collapsed 'hidden on 1' pill is the sole cue.
evidence: registry/effects.tsx:128-132 visibility styleKeys: ['display','visibility','opacity','pointer-events']; VisibilitySection.tsx:36-45 reads and writes only `--hide-${breakpointId}`; useInspectorSections.ts:161-172 seeds the open set from sectionApplies. The write itself is honoured — Canvas.css:763-767 and ExportEngine.ts:126-128 both key off --hide-<bp> — so this is a labelling/counting defect, not a dead control. Searched: '--hide-', 'hideOn', 'hideDesktop', 'hidden-desktop'.
fix: Declare the section's real keys (--hide-desktop/tablet/mobile) so 'applies', auto-expand and the footer count all describe what the section does.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user hides an element on mobile, then looks for it in the Layers tree.
finding: The Layers tree is built to show it — it draws a 'T' and an 'M' badge on any layer hidden at tablet or mobile — but the badge can never appear, because the field it reads is never populated when the tree is built. So the inspector's per-breakpoint hide has no echo anywhere outside the section that set it, and a user scanning Layers for 'what did I hide' finds nothing. Worse, Layers' own eye icon is a DIFFERENT feature (an editor-only dim that does not affect the published page), and its tooltip is the only place the product explains the difference.
evidence: LayerTreeItem.tsx:276-280 renders the badges from layer.breakpointOverrides?.mobile?.hidden / .tablet?.hidden; types.ts:49 declares the field optional; useLayerTree.ts:88-95 buildTree constructs LayerItem with id/type/tagName/depth/preview/children and never sets breakpointOverrides. LayerTreeItem.tsx:285-298 documents the eye as editor-only. Searched: 'breakpointOverrides', 'hiddenIds', 'onToggleVisibility', '--hide-'.
fix: Populate breakpointOverrides in buildTree from the element's --hide-* styles so the two panels agree, and keep the eye/publish distinction visible in both.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user switches to Tablet on an element that already has several tablet overrides.
finding: Every overridden property gets its own row PLUS its own full-width tinted banner ('Overridden on Tablet — Base is 24px'), stacked above the sections with no collapse, no summary count and no 'revert all'. Ten tablet overrides is twenty stacked blocks in a 300px-wide column before the first style control — the entire inspector is pushed below the fold, on exactly the element the user most needs to work on. There is no upper bound and no way to fold the strip away.
evidence:
BreakpointOverrides.tsx:83-128 maps every entry to a row + a

banner, unconditionally; ProInspector.tsx:501-505 mounts it above the scrolling body (:539-567), so the strip is not even inside the scroll container; the panel is a fixed 300px (LayoutShell.css:27,87 --layout-inspector-width, with no resize handle — searched 'resiz' in LayoutShell.tsx/.css: no hits). Searched: 'BreakpointOverrides', 'useBreakpointOverrides', 'getBreakpointStyle'.
fix: One collapsed summary row — '6 tablet overrides' — that expands on demand, with a 'revert all' next to it. Keep the per-row revert inside the expansion.
purpose: The right-hand inspector: read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS per breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows.

task: The user picks ':hover' and styles the hover state of a button.
finding: Picking a pseudo-state changes where every write in the panel lands, and the canvas does not change at all: nothing forces the state on the selected node, so the user edits a hover colour and sees no hover colour until they physically hover the element on the canvas — which is impossible while dragging a slider or typing in the panel. There is also no equivalent of the breakpoint-override strip for pseudo layers: a :hover rule written last week is invisible until someone thinks to pick :hover, and the only cue is a 5px dot on the state pill. The dropdown offers :disabled, :focus and :active on every element type, including plain containers, where three of the four states can never fire.
evidence: StateDropdown.tsx:19-27 five states offered unconditionally; ProInspector.tsx:433-437 mounts it, :489-499 draws the 'Editing :hover — not Base' banner (which is the only feedback); useStyleHandlers.ts:220-239 routes the write to composer.styles.setRule with the pseudo selector; computeStatesWithOverrides (config/pseudoOverrides.ts) feeds only the pill's dot. Searched for a forced-state preview: 'force-state', 'forceState', 'data-force', 'pseudo-preview', 'previewState', 'simulateState' — no hits in packages/editor/src outside one unrelated template test comment.
fix: Force the picked state on the canvas node while the state is selected (a data attribute the canvas CSS mirrors), and give pseudo layers the same 'what this state overrides' strip the breakpoints have.

task: The user needs a CSS property the panel does not expose.
finding: The raw-CSS escape hatch is registered in EVERY element profile and can never be opened from the UI: it renders only when a localStorage key is set by hand and the page reloaded. So when the panel has no control for a property, there is no way out at all — a builder aimed at people who sometimes know CSS gives them nowhere to put it. The same mechanism hides a second, parallel Border implementation behind another localStorage key, which means two Border sections are maintained and users can only ever see one of them.

task: The user changes a value and then wants to put it back the way it was.
finding: There is no reset, clear or 'back to default' on any property row, and no per-section reset either. The single revert affordance in the whole panel is the breakpoint-override strip's per-row undo arrow — which exists only when the canvas is on tablet or mobile. On desktop, removing a value means knowing that emptying the field deletes the declaration, which nothing says. Compounding it: unset rows are pre-filled with the type default or the value read off the canvas, and they look identical to values the user authored, so the user cannot tell what they have actually set.

task: The user scans the collapsed column to see what is configured on this element.

Those four also never auto-open, because auto-open is driven by CSS keys they do not have. So an element with three interactions, four classes and a link looks, collapsed, exactly like one with none of them, and nothing in the panel invites the user to open them.

task: The user removes an interaction they no longer want.
finding: Deleting an interaction is a single red button inside the expanded editor with no confirmation and no undo hint — while deleting the ELEMENT, in the same panel, opens a modal that names the element and tells the user Ctrl+Z will bring it back. Both go through composer transactions and are equally undoable, so the panel is inconsistent about the same class of action, and the cheaper of the two is the one with no safety net or explanation.

task: Whole module.
finding: PURPOSE: the right-hand inspector is the single place to read and change everything about ONE selected element — its CSS at a chosen breakpoint and pseudo-state, its HTML attributes, its link, its motion, and where it shows. PRIMARY TASKS: (1) restyle the selected element; (2) make a responsive override and see/revert what this breakpoint changes; (3) style a hover/focus state; (4) set element-specific content (image src/alt, button link, input placeholder); (5) add motion; (6) hide per breakpoint; (7) align/batch-edit a multi-selection; (8) delete/duplicate/copy-paste styles via the header ⋯ menu. ENTRY: it is always mounted in the right column (StudioPanels.tsx:494-514) — the user 'enters' it by selecting on the canvas (useSelectionBehavior, which refuses locked elements) or in the Layers tree (useLayerSelection, which does not); the crosshair 'pick element' is a third entry that also ignores locks. EXITS: hide the panel entirely (localStorage 'buildrick-inspector-shown', StudioPanels.tsx:232-244); the '✦ AI' chip, which REPLACES it with the AI tab and does not come back on the next selection (UX-D-01); 'Whole site' → Open Brand, which sends the user to the left Design panel; read-only view (?view=readonly), where the inspector is not rendered at all. HANDS OFF TO: Canvas (selection, pick mode, live style application, --hide-* preview), Brand/Design (tokens, site-wide styles), Media library and Icon picker (both opened through props threaded from the shell), CMS (BindingPopover / BindingBanner and 'Create collection'), Layers (select parent, lock/hide — where the T/M badge is broken, UX-D-19), AI panel. RECEIVES FROM: engine Composer (element set, styles, breakpoint rules, transactions/undo, component instances), shell (device/breakpoint, which is shared with the canvas, and the selected element), Layers and Canvas selection. THE SHAPE OF THE PROBLEM: the panel is strong on CSS and weak on everything a page is made of — composite elements (slider/tabs/accordion/navbar) and forms have no editor at all, while a 185-entry registry describes those editors in config; there is no search, no expand-all and no reset in a 16-section column; disabled controls do not say why; two overlapping animation systems sit next to each other; and the states that matter (locked, multi-select, whole-site, hover) are each under-drawn.
evidence: Synthesis of rows UX-D-01..28; primary files read: ProInspector.tsx (573 lines), config/elementProfiles.ts, config/propertiesRegistry.ts, config/cssContext.ts, tabs/InspectorTabContent.tsx, hooks/{useStyleHandlers,useInspectorSections,useAdvancedSettings,useInspectorState,usePickModeReset}.ts, sections/registry/{index,element,effects}.tsx, sections/interactions/*, sections/{Visibility,Link,CSSClasses,Animation,AllCSS,Variant}Section.tsx, sections/elementProperties/*, components/{MultiSelectToolbar,BatchStylePanel,BreakpointOverrides,ScopeDropdown,StateDropdown,DeleteConfirmModal,InspectorEmptyState,InspectorElementMenu}.tsx, plus shell/StudioPanels.tsx, canvas/Canvas.tsx, canvas/hooks/useSelectionBehavior.ts, panels/layers/*, engine/elements/ElementManager.ts, engine/export/ExportEngine.ts.
fix: Sequence: (1) the missing editors — composite elements and forms (UX-D-08, UX-D-09) are the only rows where the user cannot finish the job at all; (2) the lock and multi-select states (UX-D-02, UX-D-03); (3) findability — search, expand-all, reset, collapsed-state counts (UX-D-10, UX-D-11, UX-D-25, UX-D-26); (4) collapse the two animation systems into one (UX-D-14).
